claim: Learning the spatial organization of the environment is essential for most animals' survival.
source: Learning the spatial organization of the environment is essential for most animals' survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal behavior that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Spatial learning requires the animal to derive allocentric spatial information from egocentric sensory and motor experience.
source: This requires the animal to derive allocentric spatial information from egocentric sensory and motor experience.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the computational requirements of spatial learning, based on established concepts in neuroscience.

claim: The neural mechanisms underlying egocentric to allocentric transformation are mostly unknown.
source: The neural mechanisms underlying this transformation are mostly unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Electric fish can precisely navigate in complete darkness.
source: electric fish, which can precisely navigate in complete darkness
evidence: This is supported by prior research on electric fish behavior.

claim: Electric fish brain circuitry is relatively simple.
source: whose brain circuitry is relatively simple
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the complexity of electric fish neural circuits relative to other vertebrates.

claim: The preglomerular complex is the thalamic region exclusively connecting the optic tectum with the spatial learning circuits in the dorsolateral pallium.
source: the preglomerular complex, the thalamic region exclusively connecting the optic tectum with the spatial learning circuits in the dorsolateral pallium
evidence: This anatomical claim is supported by prior anatomical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: This study conducted the first neural recordings in the preglomerular complex.
source: We conducted the first neural recordings in the preglomerular complex
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental work presented.

claim: Tectal topographic information was mostly eliminated in preglomerular neurons.
source: While tectal topographic information was mostly eliminated in preglomerular neurons
evidence: This is supported by the receptive field mapping experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The time-intervals between object encounters were precisely encoded in preglomerular neurons.
source: the time-intervals between object encounters were precisely encoded
evidence: This is supported by the random interval protocol experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Reliable temporal information combined with a speed signal can permit accurate estimation of the distance between encounters.
source: We show that this reliable temporal information, combined with a speed signal, can permit accurate estimation of the distance between encounters
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling in Figures 6-8.

claim: Distance estimation between encounters is a necessary component of path-integration that enables computing allocentric spatial relations.
source: a necessary component of path-integration that enables computing allocentric spatial relations
evidence: This is based on established theories of path integration in spatial navigation.

claim: Similar mechanisms are involved in sequential spatial learning in all vertebrates.
source: Our results suggest that similar mechanisms are involved in sequential spatial learning in all vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the fish data to other vertebrates, discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: Electric fish occupied a lucrative ecological niche by evolving the ability to navigate and localize food sources in complete darkness using short-range electrosensation.
source: Electric fish, for example, occupied a lucrative ecological niche by evolving the ability to navigate and localize food sources in complete darkness using short-range electrosensation (Jun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jun et al., 2016.

claim: Electric fish exhibit spatial acuity that strongly suggests they memorize the relative arrangement of landmarks and environmental borders.
source: The spatial acuity that they exhibit, along with their reliance on learned landmark positions, strongly suggest that they memorize the relative arrangement of the landmarks and the environmental borders.
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral observations.

claim: Animals use sensory experiences collected during object encounters and motor actions executed between encounters to generate allocentric knowledge.
source: The information animals use to generate such allocentric knowledge include sensory experiences collected during object encounters (Jun et al., 2016; Petreanu et al., 2012; Save et al., 1998) and motor actions (heading changes and distance traveled) executed between such encounters
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Utilization of motor variables in spatial learning and navigation is termed path integration.
source: utilization of these motor variables in spatial learning and navigation is termed path integration (Collett and Graham, 2004; Etienne and Jeffery, 2004)
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: The information animals acquire for spatial learning is always egocentric in nature.
source: This acquired information, however, is always egocentric in nature.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the nature of sensory and motor information.

claim: The optic tectum of all vertebrates is topographically organized along an egocentric coordinate system.
source: the primary brain regions dedicated to sensory and motor processing, such as the optic tectum (OT) of all vertebrates and many cortical regions in mammals are topographically organized along an egocentric coordinate system (Knudsen, 1982; Sparks and Nelson, 1987; Stein, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Many cortical regions in mammals are topographically organized along an egocentric coordinate system.
source: the primary brain regions dedicated to sensory and motor processing, such as the optic tectum (OT) of all vertebrates and many cortical regions in mammals are topographically organized along an egocentric coordinate system (Knudsen, 1982; Sparks and Nelson, 1987; Stein, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies in the mouse have suggested that key computations for spatial learning include vestibular input that defines the animal's head direction and external sensory input that signals the presence of stable environmental features.
source: Recent studies in the mouse (Peyrache et al., 2017) have suggested that the key computations include vestibular input that defines the animal's head direction (head direction cells, egocentric) and external sensory input that signals the presence of stable environmental features (i.e., landmarks).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peyrache et al., 2017.

claim: Linking the head directions that orient the animal to different environmental features is hypothesized to generate an allocentric representation of those features.
source: Linking the head directions that orient the animal to different environmental features are then hypothesized to generate an allocentric representation of those features.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior research.

claim: The neural circuits hypothesized to implement spatial computations in mammals are exceedingly complicated.
source: The neural circuits that have been hypothesized to implement these computations are, however, exceedingly complicated and include thalamic (head direction) and cortical (external sensory) input to the hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the complexity of mammalian neural circuits.

claim: Proposed wiring diagrams for spatial computations in mammals are highly speculative and very far from providing a well-defined mechanistic model.
source: The proposed wiring diagrams are highly speculative and very far from providing a well-defined mechanistic model of how spatial maps are created.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: Equivalent computations to those in mammals appear to be carried out in Drosophila.
source: Equivalent computations appear to be carried out in Drosophila (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015.

claim: Visual orientation to landmarks and body direction via path integration are combined in the ellipsoid body of Drosophila with dynamics suggestive of a ring attractor.
source: Visual orientation to landmarks and body direction via path integration are combined in the ellipsoid body with dynamics suggestive of a ring attractor.
evidence: This is based on research in Drosophila cited earlier in the paragraph.

claim: It is not clear if the fly has a full representation of the allocentric relations of different environmental features.
source: it is not clear if the fly has a full representation of the allocentric relations of different environmental features
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: It is not clear that the dynamics of the ellipsoid body can be mapped onto the cortical and hippocampal circuitry of mammals.
source: It is also not at all clear that the dynamics of the ellipsoid body can be mapped onto the cortical and hippocampal circuitry of mammals.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of cross-species comparisons.

claim: Teleost fish offer an attractive model for studying spatial learning because their related brain circuitry is relatively tractable.
source: Teleost fish offer an attractive model for studying this question, as their related brain circuitry is relatively tractable
evidence: This is a justification for the model system used in the study.

claim: Lesion studies point to the dorsolateral pallium (DL) as the key telencephalic region required for allocentric spatial learning in teleost fish.
source: lesion studies point to the dorsolateral pallium (DL) as the key telencephalic region required for allocentric spatial learning (Broglio et al., 2010; Durán et al., 2010; Rodríguez et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to lesion studies.

claim: The dorsolateral pallium in fish is similar to the medial cortex in reptiles and the hippocampus in mammals.
source: similarly to the medial cortex in reptiles and the hippocampus in mammals (see Discussion)
evidence: This is a comparative neuroanatomical claim discussed further in the Discussion.

claim: DL has strong excitatory recurrent connectivity.
source: DL has strong excitatory recurrent connectivity (Elliott et al., 2017; Giassi et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: DL receives sensory and motor information related to electrosensory and visual object motion from OT via the preglomerular complex (PG).
source: DL receives sensory and motor information related to electrosensory and visual object motion from OT (Bastian, 1982) via a single structure – the diencephalic preglomerular complex (PG, Giassi et al., 2012b, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The tectal recipient portion of PG projects solely to DL.
source: The tectal recipient portion of PG projects solely to DL (Giassi et al., 2012a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: PG receives very little feedback from areas associated with DL.
source: PG receives very little feedback from areas associated with DL (Giassi et al., 2012b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: PG functions as an exclusive feed-forward bottleneck between OT and the pallium.
source: therefore functions as an exclusive feed-forward bottleneck between OT and the pallium
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity described.

claim: DL projects to the central pallium (DC).
source: DL in turn projects to the central pallium (DC, Giassi et al., 2012b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: DL has reciprocal connections with the dorsal pallium (DD).
source: DL also has reciprocal connections with the dorsal pallium (DD)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: DD has strong recurrent connectivity.
source: DD itself has strong recurrent connectivity
evidence: This is supported by anatomical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: DC is the only route by which DL can control motor activity.
source: DC is the only route by which DL can control motor activity
evidence: This is supported by anatomical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: DC controls motor activity solely via its projections to the OT.
source: it does so solely via its projections to the OT (Giassi et al., 2012b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: Egocentric object-related information from OT conveyed by PG to DL is converted to a learned allocentric spatial map by the recurrent circuitry of DL, DD and DC.
source: We hypothesize that egocentric object-related information (OT) conveyed by PG to DL, is converted to a learned allocentric spatial map by the recurrent circuitry of DL, DD and DC
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on anatomical and functional considerations.

claim: DC controls the fish's spatial behavior via its projections to OT.
source: DC, in turn, then controls the fish's spatial behavior via its projections to OT
evidence: This is part of the authors' hypothesis about the circuit function.

claim: PG cells emit rapid spike bursts likely mediated by T-type Ca2+ channels.
source: PG cells emit rapid spike bursts likely mediated by the T-type Ca2+ channels (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and molecular data shown in the figures.

claim: Rapid spike bursts are characteristic of the OT targets in thalamic regions of other vertebrates.
source: characteristic of the OT targets in thalamic regions of other vertebrates (Ramcharan et al., 2005; Reches and Gutfreund, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is a radical conversion of the topographic spatial representation in OT into a reliable non-topographic temporal representation of encounter sequences in PG.
source: we show a radical conversion of the topographic spatial representation in OT into a reliable non-topographic temporal representation of encounter sequences
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: The temporal information in PG is readily accessible for decoding.
source: We then use a computational model to demonstrate that this temporal information is readily accessible for decoding
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling in Figure 6.

claim: The temporal information in PG is sufficiently accurate to account for spatial precision during naturalistic behavior.
source: it is sufficiently accurate to account for spatial precision during naturalistic behavior (Jun et al., 2016)
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model predictions to behavioral data in Figures 7-8.

claim: 84 electrosensory PG cells were characterized in response to moving objects.
source: We characterized the responses of 84 electrosensory PG cells of the weakly electric fish Apteronotus leptorhynchus to moving objects
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample size.

claim: Cells responding to object motion were predominantly found in the lateral nucleus of the PG complex (PGl).
source: Cells responding to this stimulation were predominantly found in the lateral nucleus of the PG complex, PGl (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by histological verification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Only 11% of PG cells (3/27) were topographic with a spatially restricted receptive field.
source: only 11% of the cells (3/27) were topographic with a spatially restricted RF (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by receptive field mapping data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 89% of PG cells (24/27) responded across most or all of the fish's body.
source: the majority of PG cells (89%, 24/27) responded across most or all of the fish's body (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by receptive field mapping data shown in Figure 2B and supplement.

claim: PG activity does not convey a topographic 'labeled-line' code of object position.
source: Therefore, PG activity does not convey a topographic 'labeled-line' code of object position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the receptive field mapping data.

claim: The firing-rate was significantly correlated with object position in only one non-topographic cell (4%, 1/24 neurons).
source: The firing-rate was significantly correlated with object position only in one non-topographic cell (4%, 1/24 neurons; p < 0.05, random-permutations test, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutual information between object position and firing-rate was significant only in two non-topographic cells (8%, 2/24 neurons).
source: Similarly, mutual information between object position and firing-rate was significant only in two non-topographic cells (8%, 2/24 neurons; p < 0.05, random-permutations test, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by information theoretic analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Almost all PG cells have whole-body receptive fields and lack topographic spatial information.
source: Therefore, almost all PG cells have whole-body RFs and lack topographic spatial information– the hallmark of all electrosensory regions from the sensory periphery up to OT.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the receptive field and information analysis.

claim: OT electrosensory cells have spatially-restricted, topographically organized receptive fields.
source: The OT electrosensory cells driving PG have spatially-restricted, topographically organized RFs (Bastian, 1982)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: OT provides labeled-line information on the egocentric position of objects.
source: thus provide labeled-line information on the egocentric position of objects
evidence: This is an inference based on the topographic organization of OT.

claim: Only a minority of recorded PG units (26%, 7 out of 27) responded to longitudinal object motion while the object traversed their receptive fields.
source: Only a minority of recorded PG units (26%, 7 out of 27 tested with longitudinal motion) responded in this manner (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the longitudinal motion experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of PG units (78%, 20/27) exhibited a brief burst response confined to the onset and sometimes offset of object motion, but not during motion itself.
source: Rather, the majority of PG units (78%, 20/27) exhibited a strikingly different behavior, emitting a brief burst response confined to the onset (and sometimes to the offset) of object motion, but not during motion itself (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the longitudinal motion experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PG cells respond at the onset and offset of each segment of intermittent motion across the entire body.
source: This is further demonstrated when motion in each direction was broken into four segments separated by wait periods (Figure 3C), evoking responses at the onset (yellow arrowheads) and offset (red arrows) of each segment across the entire body.
evidence: This is supported by the intermittent motion experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Several lateral-line responsive PG units responded persistently throughout and even after object motion.
source: Interestingly, we have encountered several lateral-line responsive PG units that, unlike most of their electrosensory counterparts, did respond persistently throughout (and even after) object motion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by recordings from lateral-line responsive cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All PG cells recorded with transverse motion (40/40) responded to object looming.
source: All PG cells recorded with transverse-motion (40/40) responded to object looming
evidence: This is a summary of the transverse motion experiments.

claim: Only 40% (16/40) of PG cells responded to object receding.
source: while only 40% (16/40) responded to receding
evidence: This is a summary of the transverse motion experiments.

claim: Three types of responses to transverse motion were identified: proximity detection, encounter detection, and motion-change detection.
source: Three types of responses to such motion were identified: proximity detection, encounter detection, and motion-change detection
evidence: This is a categorization of the response types observed in the data.

claim: 50% (20/40) of PG cells displayed more than one type of response to transverse motion.
source: 50% (20/40) displayed more than one type of response
evidence: This is a summary of the response type analysis.

claim: 75% (30/40) of PG cells were proximity detectors that responded when an object was encountered very close to the skin (< 2 cm).
source: Proximity detectors (75%, 30/40) responded when an object was encountered very close to the skin (< 2 cm, Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by the transverse motion experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 32% (13/40) of PG cells were encounter detectors that responded when an object either entered to or departed from their electroreceptive range (~4 cm).
source: encounter detectors (32%, 13/40) responded when an object either entered to or departed from their electroreceptive range (~4 cm, Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by the transverse motion experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 57.5% (32/40) of PG cells were motion-change detectors that fired at the onset/offset of motion.
source: motion-change detectors (57.5%, 32/40) displayed a response similar to that observed in longitudinal motion, firing at the onset/offset of motion (i.e., when the object accelerated/decelerated, Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by the transverse motion experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Motion-change detector responses were relatively distance-invariant, yielding comparable responses both very close to (0.5 cm) and very far from (5.5 cm) the skin.
source: remarkably, this type of response was relatively distance-invariant, yielding comparable responses both very close to (0.5 cm) and very far from (5.5 cm) the skin despite the drastic effects of distance on both the magnitude and spread of the object's electrical image (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, see Chen et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of responses at different distances.

claim: The discrete, nearly stereotypic response in PG contrasts with the finely-tuned rate code of object distance in primary electrosensory cells in ELL.
source: This discrete, nearly stereotypic response stands in contrast to the finely-tuned rate code of object distance previously reported in the primary electrosensory cells in ELL (Clarke et al., 2014; Clarke and Maler, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research on ELL cells.

claim: The variety of PG response-types may constitute a distributed representation of object proximity.
source: Taken together, the variety of PG response-types mentioned above may constitute a distributed representation of object proximity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the response diversity.

claim: PG provides DL with coarse-grained, non-directional egocentric information about object proximity.
source: Unlike the loss of egocentric topographic mapping discussed in the previous section, this representation does provide DL with coarse-grained, non-directional egocentric information.
evidence: This is an inference about the information content of PG signals.

claim: PG electrosensory cells predominantly respond to novelty: onset/offset of object motion within their receptive field or the introduction/removal of objects into/from this receptive field.
source: We conclude that PG electrosensory cells predominantly respond to novelty: onset/offset of object motion within their receptive field or the introduction/removal of objects into/from this receptive field
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the motion response experiments.

claim: Most PG cells responded both to conductive and non-conductive objects.
source: Most PG cells responded both to conductive and non-conductive objects (Figure 4)
evidence: This is supported by experiments comparing brass and plastic spheres shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most PG cells would not discriminate between different object types, for example, plants versus rocks.
source: would therefore not discriminate between different object types, for example, plants versus rocks
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of selectivity for conductive vs. non-conductive objects.

claim: During active exploration, PG reports to the dorsal pallium whenever the fish encounters or leaves a prey or landmark or alters its swimming trajectory near a landmark.
source: We can, therefore, infer that during active exploration of the environment, PG reports to the dorsal pallium whenever the fish encounters or leaves a prey or a landmark (e.g., root mass or rock) or alters its swimming trajectory near a landmark.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of PG during natural behavior.

claim: 45% (15/33) of PG cells exhibited pronounced adaptation to repeated motion.
source: Many of the PG cells exhibited pronounced adaptation to repeated motion (45%, 15/33 neurons tested with repeated-motion protocol; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by repeated motion experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The response intensity of adapting PG cells to each encounter was strongly correlated with the time-interval immediately prior to that encounter.
source: The response intensity (number of spikes within an individually determined time window) of these adapting cells to each encounter was strongly correlated with the time-interval immediately prior to that encounter (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the random interval protocol experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant correlation between PG cell responses and intervals prior to the last one.
source: By contrast, there was no significant correlation with intervals prior to the last one (inset of Figure 5B and Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5B inset and Figure 5C.

claim: A large subset of PG cells encoded the duration of the time-interval preceding the last encounter but did not convey information about the intervals prior to that.
source: Thus, a large subset of PG cells encoded the duration of the time-interval preceding the last encounter – but did not convey information about the intervals prior to that.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal correlation analysis.

claim: The adaptation in PG is history-independent.
source: We term this history-independent adaptation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the adaptation mechanism based on the data.

claim: Similar history-independent adaptation was found in visually-responsive PG cells.
source: Interestingly, similar behavior was also found in visually-responsive cells (ventral PG, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experiments on visual cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The history-independent adaptation in PG contrasts with adaptation in mammalian cortex, where adaptation is incremental and responses depend on multiple preceding intervals.
source: This result contrasts with many studies in the mammalian cortex, where adaptation is incremental and responses depend on multiple preceding intervals (Lampl and Katz, 2017; Ulanovsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research on cortical adaptation.

claim: A spatial 'oddball' experiment revealed that adaptation in PG is spatially non-specific.
source: Moreover, a spatial 'oddball' experiment (Methods), which we conducted on 14 neurons (6 of which were adapting) revealed that this adaptation is also spatially non-specific – that is, encounters at one body location adapt the response to encounters at all other locations (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by the oddball experiments shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: The thalamic adaptation mechanism enables neurons to encode the time between the two most recent successive stimuli, without contamination by prior encounter history and irrespective of the objects' egocentric position.
source: Therefore, this thalamic adaptation mechanism enables neurons to encode the time between the two most recent successive stimuli, without contamination by prior encounter history and irrespective of the objects' egocentric position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the history-independent and spatially non-specific adaptation properties.

claim: Most PG cells were predominantly affected only by the very last time interval.
source: Hence, most cells were indeed predominantly affected only by the very last time interval.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the low β values.

claim: The fitted recovery time-scales for adapting PG cells were in the range 2.6-25.3s.
source: The fitted recovery time-scales were in the range 2.6-25.3s (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter distribution analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The response of a population of adapting PG cells to an encounter can be used to estimate the time interval elapsed prior to that encounter, using a simple, memoryless decoder.
source: We conclude that the response of the majority of PG adapting cells to an encounter can be used to estimate the time interval elapsed prior to that encounter, using a simple, memoryless decoder.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the maximum likelihood estimation simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The MLE saturated the Cramér-Rao lower error bound.
source: saturated the Cramér-Rao lower error bound (CRLB, Figure 6D)
evidence: This is supported by the error analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The estimation error increased with the decoded time interval T and baseline spontaneous activity c.
source: The error increased with the decoded time interval T and baseline spontaneous activity c
evidence: This is supported by the parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The estimation error decreased with population size N and response gain a.
source: decreased with population size N and response gain a (Figure 6E-G)
evidence: This is supported by the parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: The population of non-adapting cells (55%, 18/33) may convey sufficient information to enable estimation of global modulations and correct the temporal estimation accordingly.
source: Thus, this population may convey sufficient information to enable estimation of such confounding variables and correct the temporal estimation accordingly.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential role of non-adapting cells.

claim: Time-intervals being memorized by fish were longer in the absence of landmarks.
source: As one might expect, these intervals were longer in the absence of landmarks (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The fish's spatial error increased in the absence of landmarks.
source: This error increased in the absence of landmarks as well (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: PG is the only source of sensory information for the dorsolateral pallium (DL).
source: PG is the only source of sensory information for the dorsolateral pallium (DL), the likely site of spatial memory (Rodriguez et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on anatomical connectivity studies.

claim: History-independent adapting PG cells provide DL with one necessary component for path integration: the temporal sequence of object encounters.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that the history-independent adapting PG cells provide DL with one necessary component for path integration: the temporal sequence of object encounters (the two other components are heading-direction and linear velocity).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The simulated PG population yielded temporal and spatial estimation errors comparable to those displayed in behavior using only ~500 adapting cells.
source: The simulated PG population yielded temporal and spatial estimation errors comparable to those displayed in behavior (boxplots in Figure 8B, C), both with and without landmarks, using only ~500 adapting cells.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of model predictions to behavioral data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The lateral subdivision of PG (PGl) contains about 60,000 cells.
source: The lateral subdivision of PG (PGl), in which most motion-responsive cells were found, contains about 60,000 cells (Trinh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a cell counting study.

claim: The number of PGl cells is sufficient to attain the observed behavioral precision.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that the number of PGl cells is sufficient to attain the observed behavioral precision, even when additional encoding errors (e.g. in heading and velocity estimation) are taken into account.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the population size estimate and model predictions.

claim: Time-interval encoding in PG can consistently account for the observed behavioral precision of spatial learning.
source: Taken together, our simulations suggest that time-interval encoding in PG can consistently account for the observed behavioral precision of spatial learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling and behavioral comparisons.

claim: PG derives a sequence of discrete novelty events (encounters) from OT activity.
source: Our results suggest the following space-to-time transformation scheme: PG derives a sequence of discrete novelty events (encounters) from OT activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings about PG response properties.

claim: The history-independent adaptation process provides an accessible, accurate and unbiased representation of the time intervals between encounters.
source: The remarkable history-independent adaptation process provides an accessible, accurate and unbiased representation of the time intervals between encounters.
evidence: This is a summary of the adaptation properties and their computational implications.

claim: Visually-responsive PG cells display similar adaptation features to electrosensory cells.
source: We have found visually-responsive PG cells displaying similar adaptation features (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that this mechanism is implemented across multiple sensory modalities.
evidence: This is supported by experiments on visual cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The elimination of egocentric topographic information in PG ensures that the encoding of time is invariant to the specific body part encountering the object.
source: The elimination of egocentric topographic information in PG – both in the response itself and in its adaptation – ensures that the encoding of time is invariant to the specific body part encountering the object.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the loss of topography.

claim: The temporal information is transmitted to DL, which can use it to integrate the fish's swim velocity to obtain distance-traveled.
source: This temporal information is then transmitted to DL, which can use it to integrate the fish's swim velocity to obtain distance-traveled, a key allocentric variable.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how DL uses the temporal information from PG.

claim: The necessary velocity information for fish may be provided by the lateral-line system.
source: For fish, the necessary velocity information may be provided by the lateral-line system (Chagnaud et al., 2007; Oteiza et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on the lateral-line system.

claim: Several lateral-line responsive PG units were encountered in the recordings.
source: several lateral-line responsive PG units were encountered in our recordings (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by the recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DL can combine the distance information with instantaneous heading-direction to yield the animal's allocentric spatial position.
source: Finally, DL can combine the distance information with instantaneous heading-direction (vestibular system, Straka and Baker, 2013; Yoder and Taube, 2014) to yield the animal's allocentric spatial position (Etienne and Jeffery, 2004).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the complete path integration computation, supported by citations.

claim: A recent study in zebrafish suggests that DL neurons can process temporal information on the long time-scales discussed in this study.
source: A recent study in zebrafish suggests that DL neurons can indeed process temporal information on the long time-scales discussed here (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on zebrafish DL.

claim: The computational analysis demonstrates that the PG temporal information is sufficient to account for the spatial acuity displayed in behavioral studies of gymnotiform fish.
source: Our computational analysis demonstrates that the PG temporal information is sufficient to account for the spatial acuity displayed in behavioral studies of gymnotiform fish utilizing electrosensory information alone (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of model predictions to behavioral data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Short-range sensing used by ancestor species living in low-visibility environments necessitated the perception of space through temporal sequences of object encounters.
source: This space-to-time mechanism may shed light on the primitive basis of egocentric-to-allocentric transformations. Short-range sensing, used by ancestor species living in low-visibility environments, necessitated the perception of space through temporal sequences of object encounters.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary origins of the mechanism.

claim: With the evolution of long-range sensory systems such as diurnal vision, simultaneous apprehension of the spatial relations of environmental features became possible.
source: With the evolution of long-range sensory systems such as diurnal vision (MacIver et al., 2017), simultaneous apprehension of the spatial relations of environmental features became possible.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolution of spatial perception, supported by a citation.

claim: The neural mechanisms implementing sequential (space-to-time) spatial inference and simultaneous spatial inference presumably both exist in mammals.
source: The neural mechanisms implementing sequential (space-to-time) spatial inference and simultaneous spatial inference presumably both exist in mammals
evidence: This is a speculation about mammalian spatial processing.

claim: Clinical case studies on the regaining of eyesight in blind humans indicate that sequential and simultaneous spatial perceptions are fundamentally different.
source: Indeed, clinical case studies on the regaining of eyesight in blind humans indicate that sequential and simultaneous spatial perceptions are fundamentally different, and may therefore involve two distinct computations and neuronal pathways (Sacks, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical case studies.

claim: The population of thalamic neurons discovered may provide an essential component underlying sequential spatial learning in all vertebrates.
source: The population of thalamic neurons that we discovered may provide an essential component underlying one of these two major computations – the encoding of sequential temporal information – and we hypothesize that such neurons underlie sequential spatial learning in all vertebrates.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the generality of the mechanism across vertebrates.

claim: PG's homology to posterior thalamic nuclei is supported by anatomical and developmental findings.
source: There is substantial evidence indicating that the pathway studied here indeed has parallels in other vertebrates, and specifically in mammals. PG's homology to posterior thalamic nuclei is supported by previously published anatomical and developmental findings (Giassi et al., 2012a; Ishikawa et al., 2007; Mueller, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and developmental studies.

claim: PG's homology to posterior thalamic nuclei is supported by physiological results presented in this study.
source: as well as by physiological (Figure 1B,C) and molecular (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) results presented here
evidence: This is supported by the bursting data and molecular expression data shown in the figures.

claim: The thalamic pulvinar nucleus receives direct tectal input.
source: The thalamic pulvinar nucleus is particularly similar to PG in that it receives direct tectal input (Berman and Wurtz, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The pulvinar's involvement in visual attention and saliency in primates corresponds to PG's involvement in novelty detection.
source: Its involvement in visual attention and saliency in primates (Robinson and Petersen, 1992) corresponds to PG's involvement in novelty detection (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a comparison between pulvinar function and PG function, supported by citations and data.

claim: Pulvinar lesions are associated with saccadic abnormalities and deficits in the perception of complex visual scenes.
source: Moreover, pulvinar lesions are associated with saccadic abnormalities and deficits in the perception of complex visual scenes (Arend et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a lesion study.

claim: Pulvinar lesion deficits suggest a link to the sequential mode of spatial learning.
source: suggesting a link to the sequential mode of spatial learning
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of the pulvinar.

claim: Komura et al. (2001) demonstrated that posterior thalamic regions can implement interval timing computations over long time-scales (>>1 s).
source: Komura et al. (2001) demonstrated that posterior thalamic regions (including the rodent equivalent of the pulvinar) can implement interval timing computations over long time-scales (>>1 s)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The mechanistic basis for interval timing computations in posterior thalamus has not been identified.
source: however, the mechanistic basis for these computations has not been identified (Simen et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research, supported by a citation.

claim: Potential contributions of posterior thalamus to path integration have not been explicated.
source: potential contributions to path integration have not been explicated
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: A recent study demonstrated spatially non-specific adaptation in VPM, a posterior thalamic nucleus responding to vibrissal object encounters.
source: Finally, a recent study in rodents demonstrated spatially non-specific adaptation in VPM (Jubran et al., 2016), a posterior thalamic nucleus responding to vibrissal object encounters (Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Thalamic space-to-time mechanisms akin to those presented here play an important role in mammalian sequential spatial learning, especially in nocturnal animals relying on sparse sensory cues.
source: Taken together, we hypothesize that thalamic space-to-time mechanisms akin to those presented here play an important role in mammalian sequential spatial learning, especially in nocturnal animals relying on sparse sensory cues (Save et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the generality of the mechanism in mammals, supported by a citation.

claim: DL resembles the mammalian hippocampus in development, gross circuitry and gene expression.
source: The telencephalic target of PG, DL, resembles the mammalian hippocampus not only in function, as revealed in lesion studies (Rodríguez et al., 2002), but also in development, gross circuitry and gene expression (Elliott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The role of the hippocampus in spatial learning and navigation is well established.
source: The role of the hippocampus in spatial learning and navigation is well established
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Hippocampal neural correlates of allocentric spatial variables have been exquisitely described.
source: hippocampal neural correlates of allocentric spatial variables have been exquisitely described (Barry and Burgess, 2014; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is evidence for the importance of time coding in the mammalian hippocampus.
source: There is also evidence for the importance of time coding in the mammalian hippocampus
evidence: This is a statement about current research on hippocampal function.

claim: 'Time cells' responsive to elapsed time have been reported in the hippocampus.
source: 'Time cells' responsive to elapsed time have been reported
evidence: This is a statement about prior research on hippocampal time cells.

claim: Some hippocampal time cells also respond at specific spatial loci.
source: in some cases, these cells also respond at specific spatial loci (Eichenbaum, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A recent study on the representation of goals in the hippocampus found cells encoding the length/duration of the traveled path.
source: Furthermore, a recent study on the representation of goals in the hippocampus found cells encoding the length/duration of the traveled path (Sarel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The mechanism found in PG may contribute to creating temporal coding in the hippocampus.
source: The mechanism we have found may therefore contribute to creating temporal coding in the hippocampus, not just in the context of egocentric-to-allocentric transformations but rather whenever expectations associated with specific time intervals need to be generated.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the PG mechanism.

claim: Unlike DL's direct thalamic input via the PG bottleneck, the hippocampus receives sensory and motor information primarily via the cortex.
source: It should be noted, however, that unlike DL's direct thalamic input via the PG bottleneck, the hippocampus receives sensory and motor information primarily via the cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical differences between fish and mammals.

claim: Multiple bi-directional pathways connect the mammalian sensory and motor cortical regions with the hippocampal network.
source: Furthermore, multiple bi-directional pathways connect the mammalian sensory and motor cortical regions with the hippocampal network.
evidence: This is a statement about mammalian neuroanatomy.

claim: Pinpointing the exact loci where egocentric-to-allocentric transformations may take place in the mammalian brain is extremely challenging.
source: Pinpointing the exact loci where egocentric-to-allocentric transformations may take place in the mammalian brain is therefore extremely challenging.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in mammalian neuroscience.

claim: The egocentric-to-allocentric transformation is initiated in the mammalian thalamus where history-independent adaptation also encodes time between encounter events.
source: We propose that this transformation is initiated in the mammalian thalamus where history-independent adaptation also encodes time between encounter events.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mammalian implementation of the mechanism.

claim: Thalamic output contributes to the generation of an allocentric spatial representation in the mammalian hippocampus.
source: Finally, we propose that this thalamic output contributes to the generation of an allocentric spatial representation in the mammalian hippocampus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the role of thalamus in hippocampal function.

claim: The model implies that the fish's sense of position is critically dependent on its last encounter with an object.
source: Behaviorally, our model implies that the fish's sense of position is critically dependent on its last encounter with an object.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model.

claim: All procedures were approved by the University of Ottawa Animal Care and follow guidelines established by the Society for Neuroscience.
source: All procedures were approved by the University of Ottawa Animal Care and follow guidelines established by the Society for Neuroscience.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Apteronotus leptorhynchus fish were imported from natural habitats in South America.
source: Apteronotus leptorhynchus fish (imported from natural habitats in South America) were kept at 28°C in community tanks.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects and their origin.

claim: Fish were kept at 28°C in community tanks.
source: were kept at 28°C in community tanks
evidence: This is a description of the housing conditions.

claim: Pancuronium bromide has no effect on the neurogenic discharge of the electric organ that produces the fish's electric field.
source: which has no effect on the neurogenic discharge of the electric organ that produces the fish's electric field
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the paralytic agent used.

claim: Custom made stereotrodes or tritrodes were made of 25 μm diameter Ni-Cr wire.
source: Custom made stereotrodes or tritrodes were made of 25 μm diameter Ni-Cr wire (California Fine Wires).
evidence: This is a description of the recording electrodes.

claim: Tetrode tips were gold-plated to obtain 200–300 kOhm impedance at 1 kHz.
source: Prior to recording, tetrode tips were gold-plated (NanoZ 1.4, Multi Channel Systems, Reutlingen, Germany) to obtain 200–300 kOhm impedance at 1 kHz.
evidence: This is a description of the electrode preparation procedure.

claim: PG units were usually encountered between 2800 µm and 3400 µm ventral to the top of the cerebellum.
source: PG units were usually encountered between 2800 µm and 3400 µm ventral to the top of the cerebellum
evidence: This is a description of the recording locations.

claim: PG units were easily identified due to their characteristic rapid spike bursts.
source: and were easily identified due to their characteristic rapid spike bursts (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: This is a description of the identification criteria for PG cells.

claim: Differential extracellular voltage was obtained by using one stereotrode/tritrode channel as reference, enabling near-complete cancellation of the electric organ discharge (EOD) interference.
source: Differential extracellular voltage was obtained by using one stereotrode/tritrode channel as reference. This enabled near-complete cancellation of the electric organ discharge (EOD) interference.
evidence: This is a description of the recording technique.

claim: Only the α1G transcript of the T type Ca2+ channel (CaVT) is expressed in both PG and thalamic neurons.
source: Only the α1G transcript of the T type Ca2+ channel (CaVT) is expressed in both PG and thalamic neurons
evidence: This is supported by the molecular expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All three T-type Ca2+ channel transcripts (G, H, I) are expressed in DL and hippocampal neurons.
source: in contrast, all three transcripts are expressed in DL and hippocampal neurons
evidence: This is supported by the molecular expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PG spike bursting is generated by the α1G T-type Ca2+ channels.
source: We propose that PG spike bursting (Figure 1B,C) is generated by the α1G T-type Ca2+ channels
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the molecular expression data and physiological properties.

claim: The α1G T-type Ca2+ channel expression is a highly conserved biophysical/genetic feature of neurons in the vertebrate thalamus.
source: this is a highly conserved biophysical/genetic feature of neurons in the vertebrate thalamus
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative molecular data.

claim: 57% (24/42) of PG cells responded to both brass and plastic spheres.
source: such responses were found in 57% of the cells, 24/42
evidence: This is supported by the brass/plastic comparison experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 5% (2/42) of PG cells responded primarily to plastic with a very faint response to brass.
source: 5% of the cells, 2/42
evidence: This is supported by the brass/plastic comparison experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 38% (16/42) of PG cells responded to brass only.
source: 38% of the cells, 16/42
evidence: This is supported by the brass/plastic comparison experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The predominance of cells responding to both brass and plastic spheres or to brass-only spheres is likely inherited from OT.
source: The predominance of cells responding to both brass and plastic spheres or to brass-only spheres is likely inherited from OT (Bastian, 1982).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to prior research on OT.
